Bottom-edge bleed and not-a-discrete-object are the same defect seen from two sides — a segment that runs off the frame has no visible end, and a barrier without visible ends reads as terrain the field is made of rather than a thing standing on it (review-brief-units-topdown.md, discrete object with visible ends). The cell ships as round 5's img2img s491, which inherits e6's self-contained composition; the subject question is therefore closed without a subject change.

7._result: The axis clause worked immediately and completely — 4 of 4 seeds within 0.7 deg of top-to-bottom, zero edge bleed, on the first try — and cost the subject. Pinning the two end stakes to the frame's top and bottom edges pulls the segment to span the full height, and once six modules are sized to span 1024 px there is no room left across a 1:1 frame for a second rank, so the two overlapping ranks collapse into a single file with an oversized shield at the bottom that reads as a pointed head, i.e. as a heading, which is the one thing a barrier must not have.
7.why: e2 is the only cell in the roster re-rolled for AXIS rather than for subject or camera. It rendered diagonal (long axis 134 deg) where its siblings render top-to-bottom, and a diagonal cannot be squared up by a lossless right-angle turn: any other angle resamples the sprite and rotates its shading with it. Human ruling was to rotate e5 (a clean 90 deg) and re-roll this one. The core gains an axis statement built as a BOUNDED PAIR OF POINTS — its two end stakes pinned near the top and bottom edges — never as a run. That distinction is the whole of what four rounds taught: 'its length running from near the top of the frame down to near the bottom' tapered every wall in round 3, because naming a long line names a viewer for it to recede from, and the barrier suffix dropped axis wording entirely as a result; bounded counts are what worked instead ('six merlons' fixed e3 where 'a walk running the length' had not). Only e2's core carries the clause — e1/e3/e4 already land on axis and a working cell is not a place to test a theory.

8.why: Round 7's axis clause held but squeezed the segment to a single file, so this round added the width back as a bounded count in the same style ('three shields wide from side to side along its whole length'), one variable changed.
8._result: FAILED, and moved backwards: the on-axis seeds came out NARROWER than round 7 (aspect 0.21-0.27 against 0.25-0.27), and the one seed that did come out wide (s793, aspect 0.84) came out 40 deg off axis, exactly like the round-4 pick it was meant to replace. Across eight seeds the pattern is a hard trade rather than a wording gap: WIDE implies DIAGONAL and ON-AXIS implies NARROW. The mechanism is frame geometry, not vocabulary — a wide segment spanning a 1:1 frame's height needs more width than the frame has once its modules are sized to span it, so the only way the model can give a wide shield wall room is to lay it along the frame's diagonal. That also explains what the 'wide' renders actually are: they are wide because they are TILTED enough to show the shields' faces, whereas a rank of shields seen from truly overhead is a narrow band. The wide look is the camera drift, not the subject. Two rounds and eight seeds across two directions is the section 8.3 rung-4 stop signal for this approach; the remaining untried lever is to stop pinning the ends to the frame EDGES (pin them to the upper and lower HALVES instead) so the segment need not span the full height and has room to widen. CLOSED without spending it: the human took s794, this round's widest on-axis seed, on the reading that a narrow band is what a shield rank honestly looks like from overhead.

barrier_render_axis._note: Measured on the APPROVED shield_wall sprites (PCA long axis of the foreground mask; 0 deg = the segment lies left-to-right, 90 deg = top-to-bottom, screen y down). Every era must read TOP-TO-BOTTOM on the field, across the lane. Four of six render that way already. The two that did not are resolved the two different ways their angles deserve, by human ruling: e5 was a clean right angle, so the FREEZE SCRIPT rotates it once and ships it on axis; e2 was diagonal, where any rotation resamples the sprite and swings its shading with it, so it is re-rolled instead (round 7, seeds 691-694). The outcome is that the view needs no per-asset rotation at all — every shipped barrier is top-to-bottom — which is why `freeze_rotation_deg` exists here and `view_rotation_deg` does not. A barrier is judged on axis and has no heading, so which of the two directions a 90 deg turn takes is free.
